newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy 1998 CPI target seen as optimistic - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Italy 1998 CPI target seen as optimistic - analysts.

text.p: The Italian government's expected inflation target of 1.8 percent for 1998 seems very ambitious and is not likely to help the Bank of Italy move to adopt a softer monetary policy, analysts said.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government has set a 1998 target of 1.8 percent inflation, falling to 1.5 percent for 1999 and 2000, a trade union leader said on Wednesday.
CISL leader Sergio D'Antoni told Reuters the forecasts were contained in the government's three-year DPEF economic target plan due to be unveiled on Friday.

"A target of 1.8 percent is optimistic and will need tight monetary policy next year," said Andrea Conti of Deutsche Bank in Milan, adding he still saw a Bank of Italy interest rate cut in the near term "even if possible added-value tax (VAT) adjustments could endanger it."

The DPEF will outline the government's plans to slice 25 trillion lire off the public sector deficit in its b1998 budget by cutting spending by 17 trillion lire and boosting revenues by eight trillion lire.
One widely expected revenue-raising measure is by increasing VAT bands, in line with European levels.
Analysts said this could have a temporary impact on prices of between 0.2 and 0.5 percent, making it even more difficult to meet the 1.8 percent target for next year.

The Treasury in March set a 2.0 percent average inflation goal for next year, against a 2.5 percent target for 1997, following sharp falls over the past year. Official CPI data due out next week is expected to confirm May year-on-year inflation falling to 1.5 or 1.6 percent, its lowest level for 28 years.
Financial markets have been widely expecting the Italian central bank to reduce its 6.75 percent discount rate.
Rodolfo Dozio of Banca Commerciale Italiana, which sees an average inflation rate of 2.9 percent in 1998, said, "It will be difficult to reach the goal with a VAT adjustment."
One analyst said that a negative result of such an ambitious target was that the Bank of Italy "will have to have a more restrictive policy than currently."
Chiara Manenti of Caboto securities house agreed, seeing inflation next year at an average 2.5 percent. "These are very ambitious targets, the Bank of Italy will have be tough."
"Due to a statistical effect it is difficult to see inflation remaining so low next year, especially with a VAT rise," Conti said.
However, Lorenzo Codogno of Bank of America which sees 2.5 percent inflation next year, said "if Italy wants to enter the single European currency, the goal must be in line with European averages."

Codogno saw the Bank of Italy keeping a tight rein on monetary policy after a near-term reduction. "The Bank could cut this Friday, otherwise in June, but then it won't move for the rest of this year," he said.
But Paolo Casadio of Credito Italiano was more optimistic on the inflation front seeing a 1998 goal of 1.8 percent as possible with Italian CPI moving in line with German inflation.

"But there isn't much room for a rate cut. To keep the exchange rate stable, the differential between three-month Italian and German rates cannot fall below three percent (from 3.6 percent now)," he said, adding he thought a cut in the discount rate of 50 basis points likely by Friday.
